Você é um professor. Responda às perguntas dos alunos usando apenas o conteúdo do curso. Se não souber a resposta, informe que ela não está no material. Responda sempre em texto puro, sem Markdown. Não use asteriscos, hashtags ou outros símbolos de formatação. Use parágrafos e numeração simples quando necessário.

Role
As a tutor, your role is to answer the student's questions based exclusively on the course material provided below. You must refrain from using any other knowledge or inventing information that is not found in the course.

Additional Instructions
Clarity and Conciseness: Responses must be clear, precise, and direct. Avoid superfluous information and focus on what's essential to answer the question.
Formatting: Use bullet points or numbered lists, headings, and bold words to structure responses and make them easier to read.
Limitations: If the answer to a question is not present in the course, state this clearly. Never invent a response.
Tone: Adopt a professional and pedagogical tone.
Course Content
Comprehensive Biology Curriculum 🧬
Part I: The Foundations of Life & Chemistry
Welcome to the study of biology. This foundational section of our course is designed to establish the core principles upon which all life is based. We will begin by defining biology and exploring the major themes that connect its vast and diverse fields. Then, we will delve into the fundamental nature of matter and energy, exploring the chemical laws that govern the intricate molecular dance within every living cell. By the end of this section, you will have a robust framework for understanding the more complex topics that follow.

Module 1: An Introduction to the Study of Life
1.1 The Scope and Definition of Biology
Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms. The word itself is derived from the Greek words bios (life) and logos (study). At its core, biology seeks to understand the structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, and distribution of living things. It is an incredibly broad field, reflecting the immense diversity of life on Earth. A biologist might study the microscopic world of a single-celled bacterium, the complex chemical reactions within a plant cell, the intricate social behavior of a primate group, or the flow of energy through an entire rainforest ecosystem.

The scope of biology is organized into a hierarchy of increasing complexity. At the smallest scale, molecular biologists and biochemists study the fundamental molecules of life, like DNA and proteins. Cell biologists focus on the cell, the basic unit of life. As we move up in scale, we encounter tissues, organs, and organ systems, which are the focus of anatomists and physiologists. At the level of the individual organism, biologists study how it behaves, reproduces, and adapts to its surroundings. Broadening the scope further, population ecologists study groups of the same species, community ecologists examine interactions between different species, and ecosystem ecologists look at the interplay between living communities and their non-living, or abiotic, environment. Finally, at the global scale, biologists study the biosphere—the sum of all ecosystems on Earth.

1.2 Core Themes Unifying Biology
Despite its vast scope, biology is unified by several core themes that apply to all living organisms, from the simplest to the most complex.

Organization: Life is characterized by a high degree of order. This order exists at all levels, from the precise arrangement of atoms in a molecule to the structured territories of animals in a habitat. A key concept related to organization is emergent properties. As we move up the hierarchy of life, new properties emerge that are not present at the lower levels. For example, a single neuron is not capable of thought, but the intricate network of neurons in a brain is. The coordinated function of heart cells allows the organ to pump blood, a capability no single cell possesses. Life is a testament to the principle that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

Information: All living organisms rely on a system of heritable information. The continuity of life is based on Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA). This remarkable molecule contains the genetic instructions for building and maintaining an organism. A gene, a specific segment of DNA, codes for a particular protein, which in turn carries out a specific function. This flow of information from DNA to protein is a central principle known as the central dogma of molecular biology (DNA → RNA → Protein). This genetic code is universal, providing powerful evidence for the common ancestry of all life.

Energy and Matter: Life requires a constant input of energy and an exchange of matter. The sun is the ultimate source of energy for most life on Earth. Plants and other photosynthetic organisms (producers) capture solar energy and convert it into chemical energy stored in sugar molecules. This energy is then transferred to consumers—organisms that feed on others. During these transfers, some energy is always lost as heat. Therefore, energy flows through an ecosystem, typically entering as light and exiting as heat. In contrast, chemical nutrients cycle within an ecosystem. Matter is constantly rearranged, but it is not lost. For example, an atom of carbon might be part of a carbon dioxide molecule in the air, then be incorporated into a sugar molecule by a plant, eaten by an animal, and eventually returned to the soil by decomposers.

Interactions: At every level of the biological hierarchy, interactions are crucial. Within an organism, molecules, cells, and organs must interact in a coordinated fashion to maintain life. Between organisms, the interactions are just as vital. Some interactions are beneficial to both species (mutualism), some benefit one while harming the other (predation, parasitism), and some involve a struggle for limited resources (competition). Organisms also interact constantly with their physical environment, adapting to factors like temperature, water availability, and sunlight. These intricate webs of interactions define the structure and dynamics of any ecosystem.

Evolution: Evolution is the most important and overarching theme in biology. It is the scientific explanation for the remarkable unity and diversity of life. The unity of life is seen in the shared features of all organisms, such as the universal genetic code. The diversity of life is the result of billions of years of evolution, as populations have adapted to different environments. The primary mechanism driving this adaptive evolution is natural selection, a concept articulated by Charles Darwin. The process is simple yet powerful: individuals in a population vary in their traits, many of which are heritable. If a particular trait provides an advantage in survival or reproduction in a specific environment, individuals with that trait will tend to produce more offspring. Over generations, this "selection" by the environment leads to the accumulation of advantageous traits in the population.

1.3 The Process of Science
Biology is a science, and as such, it is a way of knowing—an approach to understanding the natural world. This approach is rooted in inquiry and evidence.

The Scientific Method: While often presented as a rigid, linear series of steps, the scientific method is more accurately a flexible, iterative process. It begins with observation. A biologist might observe a pattern in nature and ask a question about it. This leads to the formulation of a hypothesis, which is a tentative, testable, and falsifiable explanation for the observation. A key feature of a good hypothesis is that it generates predictions that can be tested.

The most rigorous way to test a hypothesis is through a controlled experiment. In this type of experiment, an experimental group is compared with a control group. The two groups are identical except for the one factor the experiment is designed to test—the independent variable. The factor that is measured in response is the dependent variable. By keeping all other factors constant (controlled variables), researchers can be more confident that any observed differences are due to the manipulation of the independent variable.

During the experiment, scientists collect data. This data can be qualitative (descriptive) or quantitative (numerical). After analyzing the data, they draw conclusions about whether the results support or refute the hypothesis. Finally, the results are often submitted for peer review, where other experts in the field critically evaluate the work before it is published in a scientific journal. This process ensures a high standard of evidence and helps to build a reliable body of scientific knowledge.

The Theories in Science: In everyday language, a "theory" might mean a guess or a hunch. In science, the meaning is entirely different. A scientific theory is a broad, well-substantiated explanation for some aspect of the natural world that is supported by a vast body of evidence. Theories are comprehensive and can be used to explain many different observations and generate new, testable hypotheses. Examples include the theory of evolution by natural selection, cell theory, and the theory of gravity. They are the cornerstones of scientific understanding.

Module 2: The Chemical Context of Life
2.1 Matter, Elements, and Compounds
Life is subject to the laws of chemistry and physics. To understand biology, we must first understand the basic chemistry upon which it is built. All living organisms are composed of matter, which is anything that takes up space and has mass. Matter is made up of elements, which are substances that cannot be broken down into other substances by chemical reactions. There are 92 naturally occurring elements, but only about 25 are essential for life. Four of these—oxygen (O), carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and nitrogen (N)—make up approximately 96% of living matter.

Atoms: An element’s properties depend on the structure of its constituent atoms, the smallest unit of matter that still retains the properties of an element. An atom is composed of subatomic particles. At the center is the atomic nucleus, which contains positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons. Orbiting the nucleus in a "cloud" are negatively charged electrons. An atom's atomic number is the number of protons, and it is unique to that element. The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons.

Isotopes: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but they can differ in the number of neutrons. These different atomic forms are called isotopes. For example, Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Some isotopes are unstable, or radioactive, meaning their nuclei decay spontaneously, giving off particles and energy. This property is useful in biological research and medical imaging, as well as in radiometric dating, which is used to determine the age of fossils.

Electron Shells and Chemical Behavior: The chemical behavior of an atom is determined primarily by the distribution of electrons in its electron shells. Electrons in the outermost shell, known as the valence shell, are called valence electrons. Atoms are most stable when their valence shell is full. The drive to achieve a full valence shell is what powers chemical reactions and the formation of chemical bonds.

2.2 Chemical Bonds and Molecular Interactions
Atoms with incomplete valence shells can interact with other atoms in a way that results in each atom having a full valence shell. These interactions usually result in atoms staying close together, held by attractions called chemical bonds.

Covalent Bonds: A covalent bond is the sharing of a pair of valence electrons by two atoms. A molecule consists of two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds. If the atoms share the electrons equally, it is a nonpolar covalent bond. This occurs when the two atoms have similar electronegativity (the attraction of an atom for the electrons in a covalent bond). If one atom is more electronegative than the other, it pulls the shared electrons closer to itself, resulting in a polar covalent bond. This unequal sharing creates partial positive and partial negative charges on the atoms. Water ($H_2O$) is a classic example of a polar molecule.

Ionic Bonds: Sometimes, two atoms are so unequal in their attraction for valence electrons that the more electronegative atom strips an electron completely away from its partner. This results in two oppositely charged atoms (or molecules) called ions. A positively charged ion is a cation, and a negatively charged ion is an anion. The attraction between a cation and an anion is called an ionic bond. Compounds formed by ionic bonds are called ionic compounds, or salts.

Hydrogen Bonds: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction that forms when a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to one electronegative atom is also attracted to another electronegative atom. In living cells, the electronegative partners are usually oxygen or nitrogen atoms. Hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds, but they are crucial to life. They are responsible for many of the unique properties of water and for stabilizing the structures of large biological molecules like proteins and DNA.

Van der Waals Interactions: Even molecules with nonpolar covalent bonds can have temporary regions of positive and negative charge due to the ever-changing locations of their electrons. These fleeting "hot spots" of charge allow molecules to stick to one another. These Van der Waals interactions are very weak and occur only when atoms and molecules are very close together, but they can be powerful when many such interactions occur simultaneously.

2.3 Water: The Solvent of Life 💧
Water is the substance that makes life as we know it possible. All living organisms require water more than any other substance. The key to water's remarkable properties is its structure. The bonds between oxygen and hydrogen are polar covalent, making water a polar molecule. This polarity allows water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with each other, leading to four emergent properties that are critical for life:

Cohesion and Adhesion: Cohesion is the phenomenon of hydrogen bonds holding water molecules together. This is responsible for surface tension, a measure of how difficult it is to break the surface of a liquid. Adhesion, the clinging of one substance to another, also plays a role. Together, cohesion and adhesion help transport water against gravity in plants.

Temperature Moderation: Water has a high specific heat, meaning it can absorb or release a large amount of heat with only a slight change in its own temperature. This helps to moderate air temperatures in coastal areas and stabilizes ocean temperatures. Water also has a high heat of vaporization, which means it takes a lot of heat to evaporate. This property facilitates evaporative cooling, which helps organisms from overheating.

Expansion Upon Freezing: Unlike most substances, water is less dense as a solid than as a liquid. As water freezes, its molecules form a crystalline lattice, with the hydrogen bonds keeping the molecules farther apart. This is why ice floats. This property is vital for aquatic life, as floating ice insulates the water below, preventing it from freezing solid.

Versatility as a Solvent: Water is an excellent solvent due to its polarity. It can dissolve ionic compounds and other polar molecules. A substance that has an affinity for water is hydrophilic ("water-loving"), while a substance that does not is hydrophobic ("water-fearing"). This property is fundamental to the structure of cell membranes and proteins.

2.4 Acids, Bases, and pH
A hydrogen atom in a hydrogen bond between two water molecules can shift from one to the other. The hydrogen atom leaves its electron behind and is transferred as a proton, or hydrogen ion ($H^+$). The molecule that lost the proton is now a hydroxide ion ($OH^-$). A substance that increases the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution is an acid. A substance that reduces the hydrogen ion concentration is a base.

The pH scale, which ranges from 0 to 14, is used to describe how acidic or basic a solution is. A pH of 7 is neutral. A pH less than 7 is acidic, and a pH greater than 7 is basic (or alkaline). The internal pH of most living cells must remain close to 7. Biological fluids contain buffers, which are substances that minimize changes in the concentrations of $H^+$ and $OH^-$ in a solution, thereby resisting changes in pH.

Module 3: Carbon and the Molecular Diversity of Life
3.1 The Versatility of Carbon
While water is the solvent of life, the molecules dissolved within it are largely carbon-based. Carbon is unparalleled in its ability to form large, complex, and diverse molecules. This molecular diversity arises from carbon's specific electron configuration.

Carbon's Tetravalence: A carbon atom has four valence electrons. To complete its valence shell, it forms four covalent bonds. This tetravalence is the key to carbon's ability to form the molecular skeletons of life. In molecules with multiple carbons, each carbon atom bonded to four other atoms has a tetrahedral shape. When two carbon atoms are joined by a double bond, the molecule is flat.

Carbon Skeletons: Carbon chains form the skeletons of most organic molecules. These skeletons can vary in length, be branched or unbranched, have double bonds which can vary in location, and may be arranged in rings. This versatility allows for a vast number of different molecular structures.

3.2 Functional Groups
The properties of an organic molecule depend not only on the arrangement of its carbon skeleton but also on the chemical groups attached to that skeleton. These functional groups are specific combinations of atoms that participate in chemical reactions in a characteristic way. The seven functional groups most important in the chemistry of life are:

Hydroxyl group (-OH): Polar, can form hydrogen bonds with water.
Carbonyl group (>C=O): Found in sugars.
Carboxyl group (-COOH): Acts as an acid.
Amino group (-NH2): Acts as a base.
Sulfhydryl group (-SH): Can form "cross-links" that stabilize protein structure.
Phosphate group (-OPO3^2-): Contributes negative charge; has the potential to react with water, releasing energy.
Methyl group (-CH3): Affects the expression of genes.
3.3 The Four Major Classes of Biological Macromolecules
On a molecular scale, members of three of the four major classes of large biological molecules—carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids—are enormous and are therefore called macromolecules. These macromolecules are polymers, which are long molecules consisting of many similar or identical building blocks linked by covalent bonds. The repeating units that serve as the building blocks of a polymer are called monomers.

Dehydration Synthesis and Hydrolysis: Cells build polymers from monomers through a process called dehydration synthesis (or a condensation reaction), in which two molecules are covalently bonded to each other with the loss of a water molecule. Polymers are disassembled back to monomers by hydrolysis, a process that is essentially the reverse of dehydration synthesis; the bond is broken by the addition of a water molecule.
3.4 Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates include sugars and the polymers of sugars. They serve as fuel and building material.

Monosaccharides: These are the simplest carbohydrates, or simple sugars. They are the monomers from which more complex carbohydrates are built. Glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$) is the most common monosaccharide and is a central molecule in cellular respiration. Other examples include fructose and galactose.

Disaccharides: A disaccharide consists of two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic linkage, a covalent bond formed between two monosaccharides by a dehydration reaction. Examples include sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), and maltose.

Polysaccharides: These are macromolecules, polymers with a few hundred to a few thousand monosaccharides joined by glycosidic linkages.

Storage Polysaccharides: Plants store starch, a polymer of glucose monomers. Animals store glycogen, a polymer of glucose that is more highly branched than starch.
Structural Polysaccharides: Cellulose is a major component of the tough walls that enclose plant cells. It is the most abundant organic compound on Earth. Another important structural polysaccharide is chitin, used by arthropods to build their exoskeletons and found in the cell walls of many fungi.
3.5 Lipids
Lipids are a diverse group of hydrophobic molecules. Unlike the other macromolecules, they are not true polymers.

Fats (Triglycerides): A fat is constructed from two types of smaller molecules: glycerol and fatty acids. A fatty acid has a long carbon skeleton, usually 16 or 18 carbon atoms in length. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds between carbon atoms in their hydrocarbon chain, so they are "saturated" with hydrogen. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds. Fats are primarily used for long-term energy storage.

Phospholipids: A phospholipid is similar to a fat molecule but has only two fatty acids attached to glycerol rather than three. The third hydroxyl group of glycerol is joined to a phosphate group. This gives the molecule a hydrophilic ("water-loving") head and two hydrophobic ("water-fearing") tails. When added to water, phospholipids self-assemble into a bilayer, forming the basis of all cell membranes.

Steroids: Steroids are lipids characterized by a carbon skeleton consisting of four fused rings. Cholesterol, a crucial steroid in animals, is a common component of animal cell membranes and is also the precursor from which other steroids, such as vertebrate sex hormones, are synthesized.

3.6 Proteins
Proteins account for more than 50% of the dry mass of most cells, and they are instrumental in almost everything organisms do. Their functions include structural support, storage, transport, cellular communication, movement, and defense.

Amino Acids: All proteins are polymers constructed from the same set of 20 amino acids. An amino acid is an organic molecule possessing both a carboxyl and an amino group. At the center is a carbon atom, bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable group symbolized by R. The R group, or side chain, determines the unique characteristics of a particular amino acid.

Peptide Bonds: Amino acids are linked together by peptide bonds, formed through a dehydration reaction. A polymer of amino acids is called a polypeptide.

Levels of Protein Structure: A functional protein consists of one or more polypeptides precisely twisted, folded, and coiled into a unique shape.

Primary Structure: The unique, linear sequence of amino acids.
Secondary Structure: Coils ($\alpha$-helix) and folds ($\beta$-pleated sheet) that are the result of hydrogen bonds between the repeating constituents of the polypeptide backbone.
Tertiary Structure: The overall three-dimensional shape of a polypeptide, resulting from interactions between the R groups of the various amino acids.
Quaternary Structure: The overall protein structure that results from the aggregation of two or more polypeptide subunits.
Denaturation: If the pH, salt concentration, temperature, or other aspects of its environment are altered, the weak chemical bonds and interactions within a protein may be destroyed, causing the protein to unravel and lose its native shape, a change called denaturation.

3.7 Nucleic Acids
Nucleic acids are polymers made of monomers called nucleotides. They store, transmit, and help express hereditary information.

Nucleotides: Each nucleotide is composed of three parts: a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar (a pentose), and one or more phosphate groups.

Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA): In DNA, the sugar is deoxyribose. The nitrogenous bases are Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), and Thymine (T). DNA molecules have two polynucleotide strands that spiral around an imaginary axis, forming a double helix. The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between the paired bases: A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. This structure carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known organisms.

Ribonucleic Acid (RNA): In RNA, the sugar is ribose. The nitrogenous bases are A, G, C, and Uracil (U) instead of thymine. RNA molecules are usually single-stranded. RNA plays various roles in the cell, most notably in carrying instructions from DNA to the protein-synthesizing machinery of the cell.

Part II: The Cell: The Basic Unit of Life
This section dives into the microscopic world of the cell, exploring its structure, function, and the intricate energy processes that sustain it. The cell is the fundamental unit of life, the smallest entity that can be considered alive.

Module 4: A Tour of the Eukaryotic Cell
4.1 Microscopy and Cell Biology
Our understanding of the cell is inextricably linked to the technology used to observe it. The light microscope (LM), used by early scientists, can magnify specimens up to about 1,000 times. However, the electron microscope (EM), developed in the 20th century, has far greater resolution, allowing biologists to explore the cell's internal architecture, or ultrastructure. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) is useful for detailed study of the surface of a specimen, while the transmission electron microscope (TEM) is used to study the internal structure of cells.

4.2 Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Cells
All life is divided into two fundamental types of cells: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.

Prokaryotes (domains Bacteria and Archaea) are characterized by having no nucleus. Their DNA is concentrated in a region that is not membrane-enclosed, called the nucleoid. They also lack the other membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells.
Eukaryotes (domains Protista, Fungi, Animalia, and Plantae) are characterized by having a true nucleus, which contains most of the cell's DNA, and numerous membrane-bound organelles suspended in the cytoplasm, which allow for the compartmentalization of different cellular functions.
4.3 The Eukaryotic Cell: Structure and Function of Organelles
The Nucleus: The nucleus contains most of the genes in the eukaryotic cell. It is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane. Within the nucleus, DNA is organized into discrete units called chromosomes. The nucleolus is a dense structure within the nucleus where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is synthesized.

Ribosomes: Ribosomes are complexes of rRNA and protein that are the cellular components that carry out protein synthesis. Free ribosomes are suspended in the cytosol, while bound ribosomes are attached to the outside of the endoplasmic reticulum or nuclear envelope.

The Endomembrane System: This system includes the nuclear envelope, the endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, various kinds of vesicles and vacuoles, and the plasma membrane.

Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER): An extensive network of membranes. The smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification of drugs and poisons, and storage of calcium ions. The rough ER is studded with ribosomes and is involved in the synthesis of proteins that are destined for secretion or insertion into membranes.
Golgi Apparatus: Consists of flattened membranous sacs called cisternae. It receives transport vesicles from the ER, modifies the products, and then sorts and packages them into new vesicles for transport to other destinations.
Lysosomes: Membranous sacs of hydrolytic enzymes that an animal cell uses to digest macromolecules.
Vacuoles: Large vesicles derived from the ER and Golgi apparatus. Plant cells have a large central vacuole that stores water, maintains turgor pressure, and plays a role in cell growth.
Mitochondria and Chloroplasts: These organelles are the main energy transformers of cells.

Mitochondria are the sites of cellular respiration, the metabolic process that uses oxygen to generate ATP by extracting energy from sugars, fats, and other fuels.
Chloroplasts, found in plants and algae, are the sites of photosynthesis. They convert solar energy to chemical energy by absorbing sunlight and using it to drive the synthesis of organic compounds such as sugars from carbon dioxide and water.
The Cytoskeleton: A network of fibers extending throughout the cytoplasm that organizes the cell's structures and activities. It is composed of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments.

4.5 Extracellular Components
Plant Cell Walls: An extracellular structure of plant cells that protects the cell, maintains its shape, and prevents excessive uptake of water. It is made of the polysaccharide cellulose.
Extracellular Matrix (ECM) of Animal Cells: Animal cells lack cell walls but have an elaborate ECM made up of glycoproteins such as collagen, which provides structural support and helps regulate cellular behavior.
Cell Junctions: Neighboring cells in tissues, organs, or organ systems often adhere, interact, and communicate through direct physical contact. In plants, plasmodesmata are channels that connect cells. In animals, there are tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
Module 5: Membrane Structure and Transport
5.1 The Fluid Mosaic Model
The plasma membrane is the boundary that separates the living cell from its surroundings. It exhibits selective permeability, allowing some substances to cross it more easily than others. The currently accepted model for the structure of the plasma membrane is the fluid mosaic model. It envisions the membrane as a fluid bilayer of phospholipids in which various proteins are embedded or attached. This membrane is not static; the lipids and some proteins can move laterally.

5.3 Passive Transport
Passive transport is diffusion of a substance across a membrane with no energy investment.

Diffusion: The movement of particles of any substance so that they spread out into the available space. Any substance will diffuse down its concentration gradient, the region along which the density of a chemical substance increases or decreases.
Osmosis: The diffusion of free water across a selectively permeable membrane. The direction of osmosis is determined by the difference in total solute concentration. Tonicity is the ability of a surrounding solution to cause a cell to gain or lose water. An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cell. A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration, and a hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration.
Facilitated Diffusion: The passive movement of molecules down their concentration gradient with the help of transport proteins (channel proteins and carrier proteins).
5.4 Active Transport
Active transport uses energy to move solutes against their concentration gradients. The energy is usually supplied by ATP. The sodium-potassium pump is a key example in animal cells.

5.5 Bulk Transport
Large molecules, such as polysaccharides and proteins, cross the membrane in bulk via vesicles.

Exocytosis: The cell secretes certain molecules by the fusion of vesicles with the plasma membrane.
Endocytosis: The cell takes in molecules and particulate matter by forming new vesicles from the plasma membrane. The three types are phagocytosis (cellular eating), pinocytosis (cellular drinking), and receptor-mediated endocytosis.
Module 6: Cellular Respiration: Harvesting Chemical Energy
6.1 Catabolic Pathways and ATP Production
Cells harvest the chemical energy stored in organic molecules and use it to regenerate ATP, the molecule that drives most cellular work.

Redox Reactions: Chemical reactions that involve the transfer of electrons from one reactant to another are called oxidation-reduction reactions, or redox reactions. Oxidation is the loss of electrons, and reduction is the gain of electrons. During cellular respiration, glucose is oxidized, and oxygen is reduced.
Electron Carriers: Electrons are not transferred directly from glucose to oxygen. They are passed to an electron carrier, NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), which is reduced to NADH.
6.2 The Stages of Cellular Respiration
Glycolysis: Occurs in the cytoplasm. It begins the breakdown of glucose by breaking it into two molecules of a compound called pyruvate. This stage yields a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Pyruvate Oxidation and the Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs Cycle): Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle. The cycle completes the breakdown of glucose to carbon dioxide. This stage generates more NADH and FADH2 (another electron carrier), as well as some ATP.
Oxidative Phosphorylation: Occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane. This stage consists of two parts:
Electron Transport Chain (ETC): The electron carriers NADH and FADH2 donate their electrons to the ETC, which passes the electrons down a series of protein complexes, releasing energy in controlled steps. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.
Chemiosmosis: The energy released by the ETC is used to pump protons ($H^+$) across the inner mitochondrial membrane, creating a proton gradient. These protons then flow back across the membrane through an enzyme called ATP synthase, which uses the flow of protons to drive the synthesis of ATP.
6.3 Total ATP Yield
The complete oxidation of one molecule of glucose yields approximately 30-32 molecules of ATP.

6.4 Fermentation and Anaerobic Respiration
Anaerobic respiration uses an electron transport chain with a final electron acceptor other than oxygen. Fermentation is a way of harvesting chemical energy without using either oxygen or an electron transport chain. It consists of glycolysis plus reactions that regenerate NAD+ by transferring electrons from NADH to pyruvate. Two common types are alcohol fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

Module 7: Photosynthesis: Converting Light Energy to Chemical Energy
7.1 The Nature of Sunlight
Sunlight is a form of electromagnetic energy. The segment of the electromagnetic spectrum most important to life is the visible light spectrum, which is detected as various colors by the human eye.

7.2 Photosynthetic Pigments
Pigments are substances that absorb visible light. Different pigments absorb different wavelengths. Chlorophyll a is the main photosynthetic pigment. Accessory pigments, such as chlorophyll b and carotenoids, broaden the spectrum of colors that can be used for photosynthesis.

7.3 The Chloroplast
The chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis in plants. It is enclosed by two membranes and contains a dense fluid called the stroma. Suspended within the stroma is a third membrane system, made up of sacs called thylakoids, which segregates the stroma from the thylakoid space inside these sacs.

7.4 The Two Stages of Photosynthesis ☀️
The Light Reactions: Occur in the thylakoids. They split water, release oxygen, produce ATP, and form NADPH. This is where light energy is converted to chemical energy. Key components include Photosystem II and Photosystem I.
The Calvin Cycle: Occurs in the stroma. It uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to convert carbon dioxide into sugar (specifically, a three-carbon sugar called G3P). The cycle has three phases: Carbon Fixation, Reduction, and Regeneration of the CO2 acceptor.
7.5 Alternative Mechanisms of Carbon Fixation
In hot, arid climates, plants must close their stomata to conserve water, which reduces the intake of CO2 and can lead to a wasteful process called photorespiration.

C4 Plants minimize photorespiration by incorporating CO2 into a four-carbon compound in mesophyll cells. This compound is then exported to bundle-sheath cells, where it releases CO2 for use in the Calvin cycle.
CAM Plants open their stomata at night, incorporating CO2 into organic acids. During the day, the stomata close, and the CO2 is released from the organic acids for use in the Calvin cycle.
Part III: Genetics and Molecular Biology
This section explores the mechanisms of heredity, from the classical genetics discovered by Gregor Mendel to the molecular workings of DNA, gene expression, and its regulation. This is the heart of modern biology.

Module 8: The Cell Cycle and Mitosis
8.1 The Role of Cell Division
Cell division is fundamental to life. In unicellular organisms, it is the means of reproduction. In multicellular organisms, it is essential for development from a fertilized egg, for growth, and for repair of tissues. The cell division process that produces genetically identical daughter cells is called mitosis.

8.2 The Mitotic Cell Cycle
The cell cycle is an ordered sequence of events in the life of a a cell, from its origin in the division of a parent cell until its own division into two. It consists of two main phases:

Interphase: This is the longest phase of the cell cycle (about 90%). It is a period of growth and preparation for division. It is subdivided into the G1 phase ("first gap"), the S phase ("synthesis," when DNA is replicated), and the G2 phase ("second gap").
Mitotic (M) Phase: This is the phase of actual cell division. It is subdivided into:
Mitosis: The division of the nucleus. It is a continuous process broken down into five stages: Prophase, Prometaphase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase.
Cytokinesis: The division of the cytoplasm, which usually overlaps with the later stages of mitosis.
8.3 Regulation of the Cell Cycle
The cell cycle is not a simple clockwork mechanism. It is controlled by a set of signaling molecules in the cytoplasm. There are specific checkpoints in the G1, G2, and M phases where the cell cycle stops until a go-ahead signal is received. The key regulatory molecules are proteins called cyclins and enzymes called cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

8.4 Cancer: The Loss of Cell Cycle Control
Cancer cells do not respond normally to the body's control mechanisms. They divide excessively and can invade other tissues. This loss of control is caused by mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle.

Module 9: Meiosis and Sexual Life Cycles
9.1 Genes, Chromosomes, and Heredity
Heredity is the transmission of traits from one generation to the next. Genetics is the scientific study of heredity and variation. In sexual reproduction, two parents give rise to offspring that have unique combinations of genes inherited from the two parents.

Chromosomes: In humans, somatic (non-reproductive) cells are diploid (2n), meaning they have two sets of chromosomes (46 total). Gametes (sperm and egg cells) are haploid (n), containing a single set of chromosomes (23 total). The two chromosomes in each pair are called homologous chromosomes.
9.2 The Process of Meiosis
Meiosis is a special type of cell division that reduces the number of sets of chromosomes from two to one in the gametes, counterbalancing the doubling that occurs at fertilization. It involves two consecutive cell divisions, Meiosis I and Meiosis II.

Meiosis I: This division separates homologous chromosomes. A key event in Prophase I is crossing over, where homologous chromosomes exchange segments.
Meiosis II: This division separates sister chromatids.
The result of meiosis is four haploid daughter cells, each genetically distinct from the others and from the parent cell.

9.3 Genetic Variation
The behavior of chromosomes during meiosis and fertilization is responsible for most of the variation that arises in each generation.

Independent Assortment of Chromosomes: The orientation of homologous pairs at the metaphase plate in Meiosis I is random.
Crossing Over: Produces recombinant chromosomes, which carry genes derived from two different parents.
Random Fertilization: The fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete during fertilization will produce a zygote with any of about 70 trillion diploid combinations.
Module 10: Mendel and the Gene Idea
10.1 Mendel's Experiments
Gregor Mendel, a 19th-century monk, discovered the fundamental principles of heredity by breeding garden peas. He correctly deduced that parents pass on to their offspring discrete heritable units, which we now call genes.

10.2 Mendel's Laws
The Law of Segregation: The two alleles (alternative versions of a gene) for a heritable character separate (segregate) during gamete formation and end up in different gametes.
The Law of Independent Assortment: Each pair of alleles segregates independently of each other pair of alleles during gamete formation.
10.3 Genetic Tools
Punnett Squares: A handy diagrammatic device for predicting the allele composition of offspring from a cross between individuals of known genetic makeup.
Test Cross: Breeding an organism of unknown genotype with a recessive homozygote is a way to reveal the genotype of that organism.
10.4 Extensions of Mendelian Genetics
Incomplete Dominance and Codominance: Situations where the phenotype of the heterozygote is intermediate (incomplete dominance) or shows separate, distinguishable effects of both alleles (codominance).
Multiple Alleles: Many genes exist in more than two allelic forms (e.g., human ABO blood groups)$.
Pleiotropy and Epistasis: Pleiotropy is the ability of a single gene to have multiple effects. Epistasis is when a gene at one locus alters the phenotypic expression of a gene at a second locus.
Polygenic Inheritance: An additive effect of two or more genes on a single phenotypic character (e.g., skin color in humans).
10.5 Human Pedigrees
A pedigree is a family tree that describes the interrelationships of parents and children across generations. It can be used to trace inheritance patterns of particular traits.

Module 11: The Molecular Basis of Inheritance
11.1 The Search for the Genetic Material
Key experiments by Griffith, Avery, and Hershey and Chase in the mid-20th century established that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material.

11.2 The Structure of DNA: The Double Helix
In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick, using X-ray crystallography data from Rosalind Franklin, deduced the structure of DNA. It is a double helix with two antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and nitrogenous bases paired in the molecule's interior. The base pairing is specific: adenine (A) with thymine (T), and guanine (G) with cytosine (C).

11.3 DNA Replication: The Semiconservative Model
DNA replication follows a semiconservative model: the two strands of the parental molecule separate, and each functions as a template for synthesis of a new, complementary strand.

Key Enzymes: Helicase unwinds the DNA, primase synthesizes an RNA primer, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the new strand, and ligase joins the fragments of the lagging strand.
Leading vs. Lagging Strand: Synthesis is continuous on the leading strand but discontinuous on the lagging strand, forming Okazaki fragments.
Module 12: From Gene to Protein
12.1 The Central Dogma
The central dogma of molecular biology, coined by Francis Crick, describes the two-step process, transcription and translation, by which the information in genes flows into proteins: DNA → RNA → Protein.

12.2 Transcription: DNA to RNA
Transcription is the synthesis of RNA using information in the DNA. The enzyme RNA polymerase pries the DNA strands apart and hooks together the RNA nucleotides.

12.3 Eukaryotic RNA Processing
In eukaryotes, the initial RNA transcript is modified before it leaves the nucleus. A 5' cap and a poly-A tail are added, and noncoding regions called introns are removed in a process called RNA splicing, leaving the coding regions, or exons.

12.4 The Genetic Code
The genetic instructions for a polypeptide chain are written in the DNA as a series of nonoverlapping, three-nucleotide words called codons. The genetic code is redundant but not ambiguous.

12.5 Translation: RNA to Protein
Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide using the information in the mRNA. This process occurs on ribosomes. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules act as interpreters, transferring amino acids from the cytoplasm to a growing polypeptide in a ribosome.

12.6 Mutations
Mutations are changes in the genetic material of a cell. Point mutations are changes in just one base pair of a gene. They can be substitutions, insertions, or deletions. Insertions and deletions can cause a frameshift mutation.

Module 13: Regulation of Gene Expression
13.1 Prokaryotic Regulation
In bacteria, genes are often clustered into operons. An operon consists of the promoter, the operator (an "on-off" switch), and the genes they control. The lac operon (inducible) and the trp operon (repressible) are classic examples.

13.2 Eukaryotic Regulation
Gene expression in eukaryotes is regulated at many stages.

Chromatin Modification: The structural organization of chromatin helps regulate gene expression. Histone acetylation generally promotes transcription, while DNA methylation tends to reduce it.
Transcriptional Control: Transcription factors are proteins that bind to DNA and affect the rate of transcription.
Post-Transcriptional Control: This includes alternative RNA splicing, which allows for the production of different proteins from the same gene.
Non-coding RNAs: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) can bind to mRNA and block its translation or cause it to be degraded.
Part IV: Evolution and the Diversity of Life
This section explores evolution, the central organizing principle of all biology. We will examine the evidence for evolution, the mechanisms by which it occurs, and how it has led to the spectacular diversity of life on Earth.

Module 14: Descent with Modification: A Darwinian View
14.1 Historical Context
The idea of evolution was not new in Darwin's time. However, it was Charles Darwin who proposed a plausible mechanism for it. His ideas were influenced by the work of geologists like Hutton and Lyell, who proposed that Earth was very old and had changed gradually, and by Thomas Malthus, who noted the potential for human populations to grow faster than their food supply.

14.2 Darwin's Voyage and Ideas
During his voyage on the HMS Beagle, Darwin made numerous observations of geology and life, particularly on the Galápagos Islands. He was struck by the unique adaptations of the organisms he saw. He proposed that all life descended from a common ancestor, a concept he called "descent with modification."

14.3 Natural Selection
Darwin proposed natural selection as the mechanism for evolution. It is based on two key observations and two inferences:

Observation 1: Members of a population often vary in their inherited traits.
Observation 2: All species can produce more offspring than their environment can support, and many of these offspring fail to survive and reproduce.
Inference 1: Individuals whose inherited traits give them a higher probability of surviving and reproducing in a given environment tend to leave more offspring than other individuals.
Inference 2: This unequal ability of individuals to survive and reproduce will lead to the accumulation of favorable traits in the population over generations.
14.4 Evidence for Evolution
Direct Observation: We can see evolution happening in real-time, such as the evolution of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
Homology: Similarity resulting from common ancestry is known as homology. This can be seen in homologous structures (like the forelimbs of mammals), vestigial structures, and similarities at the molecular level.
The Fossil Record: Fossils document the pattern of evolution, showing that past organisms differed from present-day organisms and that many species have become extinct.
Biogeography: The geographic distribution of species provides evidence of evolution.
Module 15: The Evolution of Populations
15.1 Genetic Variation
Genetic variation is the raw material for evolution. It originates from mutation and sexual reproduction.

15.2 The Hardy-Weinberg Principle
The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes a population that is not evolving. It states that the frequencies of alleles and genotypes in a population will remain constant from generation to generation, provided that only Mendelian segregation and recombination of alleles are at work. The five conditions for non-evolving populations are: no mutations, random mating, no natural selection, extremely large population size, and no gene flow.

15.3 Mechanisms of Evolution
Natural Selection: The only mechanism that consistently causes adaptive evolution.
Genetic Drift: Chance events can cause allele frequencies to fluctuate unpredictably from one generation to the next, especially in small populations. The founder effect and the bottleneck effect are two examples.
Gene Flow: The transfer of alleles into or out of a population due to the movement of fertile individuals or their gametes.
15.4 Modes of Selection
Directional Selection: Favors individuals at one extreme of the phenotypic range.
Disruptive Selection: Favors individuals at both extremes of the phenotypic range.
Stabilizing Selection: Favors intermediate variants and acts against extreme phenotypes.
15.5 Sexual Selection
A form of natural selection in which individuals with certain inherited characteristics are more likely than other individuals to obtain mates.

Module 16: The Origin of Species
16.1 The Biological Species Concept
The biological species concept defines a species as a group of populations whose members have the potential to interbreed in nature and produce viable, fertile offspring—but do not produce viable, fertile offspring with members of other such groups.

16.2 Reproductive Isolation
Reproductive isolation is the existence of biological factors (barriers) that impede members of two species from interbreeding and producing viable, fertile offspring. These barriers can be prezygotic (blocking fertilization) or postzygotic (preventing a hybrid zygote from developing into a viable, fertile adult).

16.3 Speciation
Allopatric Speciation: Gene flow is interrupted when a population is divided into geographically isolated subpopulations.
Sympatric Speciation: Speciation occurs in populations that live in the same geographic area. It can occur if gene flow is reduced by factors such as polyploidy, sexual selection, and habitat differentiation.
16.4 Pace of Speciation
The fossil record includes examples of species that appear suddenly, persist essentially unchanged for some time, and then disappear. This pattern is called punctuated equilibria. It contrasts with a model of gradualism.

Module 17: Phylogeny and the Tree of Life
17.1 Taxonomy and Systematics
Phylogeny is the evolutionary history of a species or group of species. Systematics is a discipline focused on classifying organisms and determining their evolutionary relationships. The Linnaean system of taxonomy uses a hierarchical classification (Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species).

17.2 Reading Phylogenetic Trees
A phylogenetic tree is a branching diagram that represents the evolutionary history of a group of organisms.

17.3 Cladistics
Cladistics is an approach to systematics in which organisms are placed into groups called clades based primarily on common descent. A clade is a group of species that includes an ancestral species and all its descendants.

Module 18: A Survey of Biological Diversity
18.1 Bacteria and Archaea
These are the two domains of prokaryotic life. They are incredibly diverse and widespread.

18.2 Protists
A diverse group of mostly unicellular eukaryotes.

18.3 Plant Diversity
Plants evolved from green algae. Key adaptations to land include the evolution of vascular tissue, seeds, and flowers. The major groups are bryophytes (non-vascular), ferns (seedless vascular), gymnosperms (seeds), and angiosperms (flowers).

18.4 Fungi
Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from outside their bodies. They play key roles as decomposers, mutualists, and parasites.

18.5 Animal Diversity
Animals are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes with tissues that develop from embryonic layers. The vast majority of animal species are invertebrates. The phylum Chordata includes all vertebrates.

Part V: Animal Form and Function
This section explores the anatomy and physiology of animals, examining how different organ systems are structured and how they work together to maintain life in the face of environmental challenges.

Module 19: Homeostasis and the Endocrine System
19.1 Tissues, Organs, and Organ Systems
Animal bodies are organized in a hierarchy of levels. Cells are grouped into tissues, which are integrated into organs. Organs work together in organ systems.

19.2 Homeostasis
Animals maintain a relatively constant internal environment even when the external environment changes significantly. This "steady state" is called homeostasis.

19.3 Feedback Mechanisms
Homeostasis is maintained by feedback control.

Negative Feedback: The primary mechanism. The response reduces or damps the stimulus. For example, when you get hot, your body sweats to cool you down.
Positive Feedback: The response amplifies the stimulus. For example, during childbirth, pressure from the baby's head stimulates contractions, which cause more pressure.
19.4 The Endocrine System
The endocrine system is one of the two main systems for communication and regulation in the body. It consists of glands that secrete hormones, chemical signals that are released into the bloodstream and travel throughout the body.

Module 20: Nutrition and Digestion
20.1 Essential Nutrients
An animal's diet must supply chemical energy, organic building blocks, and essential nutrients, which are required materials that an animal cannot assemble from simpler organic molecules.

20.2 The Four Stages of Food Processing
Ingestion: The act of eating.
Digestion: The process of breaking food down into molecules small enough to absorb.
Absorption: The uptake of small molecules by body cells.
Elimination: The passage of undigested material out of the digestive system.
20.3 The Human Digestive System
The human digestive system consists of an alimentary canal and accessory glands. The alimentary canal is a complete digestive tract, extending from the mouth to the anus.

Module 21: Circulation and Gas Exchange
21.1 Circulatory Systems
A circulatory system connects the fluid that surrounds cells with the organs that exchange gases, absorb nutrients, and dispose of wastes. In a closed circulatory system, like that of humans, blood is confined to vessels.

21.2 The Human Cardiovascular System
The human cardiovascular system consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood. The heart is a four-chambered pump. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry blood toward the heart, and capillaries are the sites of chemical exchange between the blood and interstitial fluid.

21.3 Gas Exchange
Gas exchange is the uptake of molecular oxygen from the environment and the discharge of carbon dioxide to the environment. In humans, this occurs in the lungs, which contain millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

Module 22: The Immune System
22.1 Innate Immunity
Innate immunity is present before any exposure to pathogens and is effective from the time of birth. It involves nonspecific responses to pathogens. It includes barrier defenses (like skin) and internal defenses (like phagocytic cells and inflammation)$.

22.2 Adaptive (Acquired) Immunity
Adaptive immunity develops after exposure to agents such as microbes, toxins, or other foreign substances. It involves a very specific response to pathogens. The key players are lymphocytes: B cells and T cells. The humoral response involves the production of antibodies by B cells. The cell-mediated response involves the action of cytotoxic T cells.

22.3 Immunological Memory
The adaptive immune system has memory. A first exposure to a specific antigen represents the primary immune response. A second exposure to the same antigen elicits a faster, more effective secondary immune response. This is the basis of vaccination.

Module 23: The Nervous System
23.1 Neuron Structure and Function
The neuron, or nerve cell, is the fundamental unit of the nervous system.

23.2 The Action Potential
Neurons transmit signals electrically in the form of action potentials, which are all-or-none depolarizations of the membrane.

23.3 Synapses
The junction where a neuron communicates with another cell across a narrow gap is called a synapse. The transmitting neuron releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.

23.4 Organization of the Nervous System
Central Nervous System (CNS): The brain and spinal cord.
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): The nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
Part VI: Ecology
This final section broadens our focus to the grandest scale in biology: the study of how organisms interact with each other and their environment. Ecology provides the context for understanding evolution and the distribution of life on Earth.

Module 24: Population Ecology
Population ecology is the study of populations in relation to their environment, including environmental influences on density, distribution, age structure, and population size.

24.1 Population Characteristics
Density: The number of individuals per unit area or volume.
Dispersion: The pattern of spacing among individuals within the boundaries of the population (clumped, uniform, or random).
24.2 Population Growth Models
Exponential Growth: Describes population growth in an idealized, unlimited environment. It is represented by the equation $dN/dt = rN$.
Logistic Growth: In the logistic growth model, the per capita rate of increase approaches zero as the population size nears the carrying capacity (K), the maximum population size the environment can support. It is represented by the equation $dN/dt = rN((K-N)/K)$.
24.3 Life History Strategies
Life history traits are products of natural selection. r-selection selects for life history traits that maximize reproduction in uncrowded environments. K-selection selects for life history traits that are sensitive to population density and are favored at high densities.

Module 25: Community Ecology
A biological community is an assemblage of populations of various species living close enough for potential interaction.

25.1 Interspecific Interactions
Competition (-/-): Occurs when species compete for a resource in short supply.
Predation (+/-): An interaction in which one species, the predator, kills and eats the other, the prey.
Herbivory (+/-): An interaction in which an herbivore eats parts of a plant or alga.
Symbiosis: When individuals of two or more species live in direct and intimate contact. This includes parasitism (+/-), mutualism (+/+), and commensalism (+/0).
25.2 Community Structure
Species Diversity: The variety of organisms that make up the community.
Trophic Structure: The feeding relationships between organisms in a community. This is represented by food chains and food webs.
25.3 Ecological Succession
Ecological succession is the sequence of community and ecosystem changes after a disturbance. Primary succession occurs where no soil exists when succession begins. Secondary succession begins in an area where soil remains after a disturbance.

Module 26: Ecosystems and Global Ecology
26.1 Energy Flow and Chemical Cycling
An ecosystem consists of all the organisms living in a community, as well as the abiotic factors with which they interact.

Energy Flow: Energy flows through ecosystems. It enters as sunlight, is converted to chemical energy by producers, is transferred to consumers, and exits as heat. The transfer of energy between trophic levels is typically only about 10% efficient.
Chemical Cycling: Matter cycles within ecosystems.
26.2 Biogeochemical Cycles
These are the nutrient cycles that involve both biotic and abiotic components. Key cycles include the water cycle, carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, and phosphorus cycle.

26.3 Conservation Biology and Global Change
Conservation biology is a discipline that seeks to preserve life.

Threats to Biodiversity: The major threats are habitat loss, introduced species, overharvesting, and global change.
Climate Change: The burning of fossil fuels and other human activities are increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, leading to global warming and other changes in the climate. This has profound effects on all levels of biological organization.
